property_summary: For any caller who is the admin, calling setOwner(_owner) updates the public owner state to equal the provided _owner; the mutant that omits the assignment breaks this by leaving owner unchanged for some fuzzed _owner inputs.

For any caller address used by the admin to call setOwner(_owner), the reference contract always sets owner to the provided _owner parameter; the mutant instead sets owner to tx.origin, so when the admin calls via a forwarding contract (making tx.origin != the immediate caller) the mutant will set owner to tx.origin and thus differ from the provided _owner.

For any address admin that calls setOwner(via a forwarder contract), the reference contract sets owner to the provided _owner argument (owner == _owner), while the mutant sets owner to tx.origin causing owner != _owner when the call is proxied through a forwarder (tx.origin != msg.sender).

When the admin calls setOwner through any caller, the correct contract always sets owner to the provided _owner argument; the mutant instead sets owner to tx.origin, so for a proxied call (where tx.origin != _owner) the mutant can make owner differ from the provided _owner.

For any caller that is the admin, calling setOwner(_owner) results in c.owner() == _owner in the reference; the mutant that assigns tx.origin instead can produce c.owner() != _owner when the admin's call is proxied through a forwarder (so tx.origin differs), which the fuzzer can find by providing a proxying forwarder address and admin input.

Rule: Only the original admin (the deployer) can call setOwner; thus for any caller address A != admin, a call to setOwner(A) must revert (or not change owner) in the reference, whereas the mutant that checks owner instead of admin allows the current owner to call setOwner and so can change owner when msg.sender == owner but not admin, violating the rule for some fuzzed owner address.

For every caller address X and newOwner Y, only the original admin (the deployer) can successfully call setOwner(Y) and change C.owner; the mutant that compares msg.sender to owner instead of admin allows a call by the current owner (when owner != admin) to change owner, violating this rule for some fuzzed addresses.

For every caller Addr and candidate newOwner, only the original deployer (admin) can successfully execute setOwner(newOwner) (i.e. a call to setOwner by any address other than the deployer must not change C.owner); the mutant that checks msg.sender==owner instead of admin allows a non-deployer who is the current owner to call setOwner and change owner, violating this rule for some fuzzed inputs.

For every caller addr and candidate newOwner, only the original deployer (the admin, set at construction) can successfully change C.owner via setOwner; the mutant that compares msg.sender to owner instead of admin allows the current owner (when different from admin) to change owner, violating this rule for some fuzzed inputs.

Rule: Only the original deployer (the stored admin) can successfully change the contract's owner via setOwner; the mutant that compares msg.sender to owner instead of admin allows calls by the current owner (when different from admin) to change owner, so there exist fuzzed caller and newOwner addresses that make the mutant change owner while the reference does not.

For any caller who is the admin, calling setOwner(...) completes (does not revert) and returns true; the mutant still completes but may return false so its return value can differ from true for some admin caller and owner argument.

For every caller/admin and owner address, calling setOwner as the admin returns true (the reference always returns true on successful completion); the mutant that omits the explicit return can complete but will return false for some inputs, thus violating this rule.

For any admin caller and target owner address, a successful call to setOwner completes and returns true in the reference contract; the mutant that omits the explicit return may still complete but return false for some inputs, violating this rule.

For every caller address, calling setOwner(...) on the reference contract reverts unless the caller is the admin (only admin can successfully call and update owner); the mutant allows non-admin callers to succeed, breaking this authorization property for some caller addresses.

For any caller and any address input, only the contract's admin (the deployer) is able to change c.owner via setOwner; the mutant removes this restriction so some non-admin callers can change owner and thus violate the rule.

For any caller address chosen by the admin when invoking setOwner(_owner), the correct contract always sets owner to the provided _owner argument, whereas the mutant instead sets owner to msg.sender (the admin), thus changing owner whenever _owner != msg.sender.

For any caller that is the admin, calling setOwner(x) results in owner == x in the reference; the mutant instead makes owner == msg.sender when x != msg.sender, so the property is that owner equals the supplied argument after setOwner is called by the admin.

For every caller and target owner address, only the original admin (deployer) can successfully change owner via setOwner; the mutant that allows the current owner to also call setOwner can be used by a non-admin who is the owner to change ownership (violating the rule).

Invariant: only the original admin (the contract deployer) can call setOwner to change owner; the mutant allowing the current owner to also call setOwner breaks this because a non-admin who has been made owner can further change owner.
